This pronounced sexual size dimorphism is a common pattern among ranid frogs and likely reflects strong fecundity selection on females, as larger body size permits the production of larger clutches. Males, in contrast, achieve sexual maturation at a smaller body size, with puberty occurring when they reach 4.22 centimeters [Lp = 4.22 centimeters] in snout–vent length. This early maturation allows males to begin competing for breeding opportunities sooner, although they continue somatic growth thereafter. The species thus exhibits a life-history strategy in which females delay reproduction relative to males to attain a larger adult size, whereas males trade off further growth against earlier reproductive activity. These size thresholds are critical for understanding population dynamics and have been derived from long-term mark–recapture studies across multiple breeding seasons in the southeastern United States.

Female southern leopard frogs achieve an ultimate wet weight of 148.4 grams [Wwi = 148.4 grams], a value scaled from body size relationships in related ranid species and consistent with the large clutch sizes they produce. This striking difference in mass between the sexes translates into divergent energetic budgets: a gravid female may invest a substantial fraction of her body mass into a single clutch of eggs, whereas males allocate relatively less to gamete production and more to territorial defense and chorus attendance. The species thus exemplifies a pattern common in explosively breeding anurans, where males maximize mating opportunities through early arrival at breeding sites and prolonged calling effort, while females optimize fecundity through delayed maturation and continued growth after reaching puberty.
